Novaspace CEO Pacome Revillon presented forecasts showing defense space budgets climbing to $121B by 2028 (from $74B in 2025) and ISR satellite launches quadrupling this decade. Space-tech VC hit $11.3B in H1 2026 alone.

Open Cosmos closed a €300M Series C days before the conference, crossing into unicorn territory and explicitly earmarking the funds to scale engineering, manufacturing, and software teams across four countries. 

Eutelsat CEO Jean-François Fallacher expanded its Airbus order to 669 OneWeb satellites plus 264 for Europe's IRIS² constellation.

Funded scale-ups are hiring hard across engineering, manufacturing, and software, but the market has a real experience cliff. Mid-career systems engineers, flight software, propulsion, and RF specialists are in short supply, and clearance requirements are stretching timelines further.

A rushed technical hire rarely fails in week one.

It fails in month four, when nobody remembers the decision was made in a hurry.

The pressure is real. A roadmap slips, a client is waiting, a key engineer resigns. So the bar drops a little, and "good enough" becomes the standard.

The cost shows up later, and not on any hiring dashboard:

Senior engineers spend more time on reviews and rework, so their own output drops first.
Small shortcuts in design add up to tech debt someone pays for next year.

Onboarding gets rushed too, so the new hire stays unsure and the team stays cautious.

Strong people get tired of cleaning up after weak fits, and some leave.

AI adds a new twist. Coding assistants can make an average engineer look productive on routine tasks, and that speed is genuinely useful. But they don't replace judgement on architecture, trade-offs, or knowing when generated code is wrong. That judgement is harder to spot in a quick interview, which makes rushed hiring riskier, not safer.

A few things help when time is short:

-Define the problem before the job title.
-Test how people reason, not only what they have built.
-Use a short contract or contract-to-hire period when the need is urgent but unclear.
-Keep the bar where it was, even when the deadline moves.
-The teams that hire well under pressure usually did one thing early. They decided what a good hire looks like before the pressure started.

You only have to search LinkedIn, job boards, anywhere, and type in "AI" or "Artificial Intelligence" to see an abundance of roles being advertised right now. It's not surprising given the UK's AI sector alone now comprises over 5,800 businesses generating roughly £24 billion a year. Everyone wants to be involved with, or using, AI in some capacity, and that can be considered both a blessing and a curse.

From a client perspective, more candidates wanting to align their focus into AI means more people applying for every AI role posted, which means more work for internal talent teams sifting through it all. Recent research shows "AI user" roles, people applying AI within an existing job function, are growing nearly three times faster than genuine AI "developer"/specialist roles (65.8% vs 21.6% YoY). The impact? It means a lot of that application volume is candidates repositioning toward AI language rather than people who can actually build and ship it, and the very best of the best are often not the ones actively applying at all. This means the real question isn't how many CVs came in; it's whether you're actually reaching the top talent, or just the most active job seekers.

From a candidate perspective, more jobs on the surface looks great, but what a company says it's doing with AI and the reality on the ground are often two very different things. ONS figures show AI adoption among UK businesses has nearly tripled since 2023, from around 12% to 35%; but among the businesses that have adopted it, the average one is only using 1.6 AI technologies, and just 11% have trained more than half their workforce on it. The headline number is growing fast; the depth behind it isn't keeping pace. A business can have all the right intentions, but if the foundations, data, skills, structure, aren't in place yet, no amount of ambition alone gets you to a successful outcome, or a role that lives up to what was advertised.

What is $BWET actually tracking?
It holds crude oil tanker freight futures — contracts tied to the cost of hiring supertankers (VLCCs) to move crude from the Middle East to China, and from West Africa to Europe. It doesn't hold oil, ships, or energy stocks. It's a pure bet on shipping cost.

⛽ Diesel and crude transport costs are already spilling into record-high diesel prices at the pump, squeezing farmers, truckers and consumers alike.

The report doesn't put this on one cause, and the detail is worth sitting with. In large parts of the world, there simply aren't enough entry-level roles being created each year to absorb the number of young people leaving school.

Millions more are working, just not in anything that leads anywhere – a day of gig delivery with no contract and no route to something better. A teenager in a town with patchy internet can't finish the same online course, let alone build the same portfolio, as one in a city with fibre broadband.

Young women are pulled out of the workforce entirely far more often than young men – two out of every three people in this group. And sure- AI plays a role too… the same report puts AI-driven task exposure among young workers at around 6%.

It strikes me in so many of these situations it’s not about young people being lazy or at fault here. Most of them were never given the real skills required to meet any employer's hiring bar in the first place.

That's the distinction for me –  and what motivates us at Lynx – we upskill underserved groups, but I know a training programme or schooling that ends in just a diploma or a certificate is not the same as one that ends in an interview.

If those funding these programmes – including companies like ours, alongside government providers aren't building toward an outcome an employer will actually hire against, we're just producing a different kind of idle time with a certificate stapled to it.

A stat like this can read as a wall. I'd rather read it as a list of exactly where the doors are missing, and go build a few more.

Talent acquisition (TA) has transformed from a transactional, administrative hiring process into a strategic, data-driven, and technology-centered business driver.  
​Where recruiting once relied on reactive job postings, resume stacks, and localized candidate pools, modern talent acquisition operates as a continuous, proactive engine focused on skills, candidate experience, and long-term workforce planning.  

Core Drivers Defining Modern Talent Acquisition
​1. Shift to Skills-Based Hiring
​Organizations are increasingly dropping rigid degree requirements and specific job title histories in favor of skills verification. Practical assessments, portfolios, and AI-driven skill mapping allow companies to expand candidate pools, improve diversity, and hire for adaptability over pedigree.  
​2. Artificial Intelligence & Automation
​AI has reframed how recruiters work by handling high-volume, repetitive tasks:
​Automated Screening & Sourcing: Matching algorithms scan large talent pools to surface candidates based on contextual fit rather than basic keyword matching.
​Conversational Assistants: AI chatbots handle initial screening calls, answer applicant FAQs, and coordinate interview scheduling 24/7.  
​Predictive Workforce Analytics: Data models forecast attrition, identify future skill gaps, and optimize candidate acquisition channels based on past hiring outcomes.  
​3. Borderless & Flexible Talent Pools
​Remote and hybrid work models have uncoupled talent acquisition from geography. Companies engage borderless workforces using:  
​Global Hiring Platforms (Employer of Record/EOR): Allowing organizations to hire legally in countries without setting up physical entities.  
​Blended Workforce Models: Integrating full-time employees alongside contract, gig, and fractional specialists to scale capacity dynamically.
​4. Recruitment Marketing & Employer Branding
​Job seekers now evaluate employers much like consumers evaluate products. Modern TA functions use marketing methodologies to attract talent:
​Targeted Campaigns: Social media, candidate-focused content, and authentic employee stories replace dry job descriptions.  
​Focus on Values & Culture: Candidates prioritize transparency, company mission, career progression, and flexibility.  
​5. Diversity, Equity, & Inclusion (DEI) as a Core Metric
​Modern TA relies on structured interviewing, blind screening tools, and demographic analytics to reduce human bias, broaden sourcing channels, and build balanced teams.

A radiologist named 𝗚𝗲𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗻, one of the founding figures of modern AI, said in 2016 that hospitals should stop training radiologists because AI would replace them within five years. Nearly a decade later, radiology hiring is still growing. The technical reason he was wrong is one worth understanding before believing any bold AI replacement claim.

The core problem: Hinton was reasoning from a single benchmark, AI models were beating human radiologists at spotting tumors in isolated medical images under controlled test conditions. What that benchmark quietly left out was almost everything else the job actually involves.

Here is what the benchmark missed technically:
𝟭. The test measured 𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 on a single, clean, well labeled image, not the full job. A radiologist's real work includes weighing a patient's history, comparing scans over time, catching rare edge cases nothing like the training data, and explaining findings to a worried patient face to face.
𝟮. This gap has a name, 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝘃𝘀 𝗷𝗼𝗯 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. AI models get benchmarked and often win on narrow, well defined tasks. Real jobs are usually a bundle of dozens of tasks, many of them messy, contextual, and poorly defined, exactly where models still struggle.
𝟯. What actually happened in practice was not replacement, it was 𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. AI now flags suspicious regions on a scan first, and the radiologist reviews that flagged output faster than reading the whole image cold, then applies judgment the model cannot. The job did not disappear, the workflow shifted.
𝟰. Benchmarks are also usually run on clean, curated test images. Real world scans include motion blur, unusual patient anatomy, and equipment variation the benchmark never had to handle, which is exactly where the accuracy gap between "test score" and "real deployment" tends to show up.

The scenario that makes this click: imagine judging whether a translator's job is obsolete purely because software translates a simple restaurant menu perfectly. That says nothing about whether it can handle a nuanced legal contract, a poem, or a tense negotiation, the actual bulk of what a professional translator handles day to day.

The lesson beyond radiology: whenever you see a claim that "AI beats humans" at a job, check whether it beat humans at the whole job or one narrow, cleanly measured slice of it. Almost every confident replacement prediction in AI's history has made exactly this mistake, mistaking a benchmark win for a job replacement.

Separating a clean benchmark result from real, messy production performance is exactly the kind of gap our audits are built to surface before a company bets real budget on it.

McKinsey just killed the case for building your own AI.

Their July 2026 AEC report has one sentence buried in it that reverses a decade of construction tech strategy.

"AEC firms have historically struggled to build and scale software products, and AI is advancing too quickly for most incumbents to rely primarily on internal development."

Read that twice.

For years, the accepted logic in construction leadership was clear. Own your stack. Build the moat. Proprietary tools protect margin.

That logic just broke.

Here is why.

The model release cycle for foundation AI is now measured in months. GPT, Claude, and Gemini all shipped material capability jumps in the last two quarters. Your internal dev team cannot match that velocity. No dev team can.

Meanwhile, the workflows that generate real construction ROI (document query, contract review, cost variance forecasting, scope generation) are already being solved by specialist vendors with 100x your training data.

The maths gets uncomfortable fast.

Building a proprietary AI system for a mid-market GC costs £400K to £1.2M over 18 months. By the time it ships, three commercial products have overtaken it. Your team is now maintaining a depreciating asset while running projects with worse tools.

McKinsey's alternative is partner-first. Buy the commodity layer. Configure the workflow layer. Own only the data layer.

Translated:

1. Foundation models are commodities. Rent them.

2. Workflow tools are configurable. Tune them.

3. Your project data is proprietary. Own it, structure it, protect it.

The moat moved.

It used to sit inside your software. It now sits inside your data pipeline and how well your team uses off-the-shelf tools against it.

Firms still budgeting to build internal AI in 2026 are solving 2019's problem.

The 5% of construction firms getting real ROI from AI (per MIT and BCG) all share this posture. They partner on capability, invest heavily in data readiness, and treat vendor selection as a core competency rather than a procurement task.

If your current AI plan involves hiring a team of ML engineers, stop and read the McKinsey report before you sign the offer letters.

The strategic answer changed. The firms that catch up first win the next decade.
